title: Chapter 46: Rowan Writes Back, Part 1 of 5: Juno
html:
Juno came at the eighth bell, walking on the sides of her feet.
Lyra saw her from the far end of the crypt. She was on her knees by a pallet near the blanketed door, with a bowl of warm water and a cloth, washing the face of the girl who watched the lamp. The girl was called Polly. Mrs. Doyle had told her that this morning. Polly was six, and she had not blinked yet today, and when you washed her face she did not shut her eyes against the water the way any child would. She only watched the lamp, and let the water run into her eyes, and did not seem to feel it.
The low door at the far end of the crypt opened, and let in a slab of gray light and a gust of snow, and a small figure in a cap.
Lyra knew her by the way she stood. Before the face. Before anything. A small square shape in the doorway with its feet apart and its fists at its sides, the way a boy stands at the top of a wall before he jumps off it. And then the shape moved, and came in, and Lyra saw how it moved, and put down her cloth.
Juno was walking on the outsides of her feet.
Not limping. It was worse than a limp. She came down the long low hall between the pillars with her ankles turned out and her weight on the very edges of her boots, the way you walk on a beach full of sharp stones, carefully, one foot and then the other, with her arms held out a little from her sides for balance. Every step, her face did something. Not a wince. Something smaller and quicker than a wince, and then gone, and then again at the next step.
She had walked fourteen miles on those feet, a week ago, in the snow, across twenty-three bridges and three locks, to bring Lyra a catalogue. Lyra had held them in her lap that night, on the barge, wrapped in a blanket, and felt how cold they were. White to the ankle. Like marble.
She got up.
She did not run this time. She had run down the Steps on Tuesday night, and fallen on the ice, and there was a bruise on her knee the size of a saucer to show for it. She walked. Down the hall between the pallets, past the braziers, past Mrs. Fitch bent double over a bucket, and she met Juno halfway, by the fourth pillar, under its lamp.
They looked at each other.
Juno's face was red with cold, and shining, the way it always shone after a run, and her cap was pushed back off her forehead. Her nose was running. She wiped it on the back of her hand. Her eyes were very bright. Then she looked at Lyra's hair, under Ellis's cap, the cropped ends sticking out over the ears.
"You cut it," she said.
"I sold it."
Juno looked at it for a moment longer.
"It's all right," she said. "It'll grow." She sniffed. "Mine got cut once. When I had nits. Gran did it with the bread knife. I looked like a boiled egg." She looked down at her own boots. Then up again. "My feet are all right. Before you ask. They hurt. That's good. Wat says when they stop hurting is when you worry."
Lyra did not say anything. She put her arms round Juno and held her.
She had never done that before. She did not know if Juno would like it. Juno was not a girl who liked things like that, Lyra thought. She was a girl who ran over roofs and sat on the edges of water troughs and swung her boots and said rude things to constables. But Juno did not pull away. She stood very still in Lyra's arms, by the fourth pillar, under the lamp, in the smell of pears, with her fists at her sides. And then, after a moment, one of the fists came up, and took hold of the back of Lyra's coat, and held on.
"Hessa says," said Juno, into Lyra's shoulder, "that if you've got yourself killed she'll never speak to you again."
"I haven't."
"I can see that." Juno let go of the coat. She stepped back, and wiped her nose again, and looked round at the crypt. At the pillars, and the lamps, and the long rows of pallets, and the children lying on them. At the smell. Her face changed. "Oh," she said. Very quietly. "Oh. This is where they are."
"Yes."
Juno looked at the nearest pallet. At Polly, lying with her wet face, watching the lamp.
"I knew some of them," she said. "From the Docks. I didn't know they'd come here." She swallowed. "There's Kit Flynn. By the wall. He used to steal apples off the barrows on Fish Street and throw the cores at the gulls. He had the best arm in the Lower Docks." She looked at the boy by the wall, turning his wooden spoon over and over in his hands. "He doesn't know me. Does he."
"Not yet," said Lyra. "The doctor says—maybe in a month."
Juno nodded slowly.
Then she turned her back on the pallets, deliberately, the way you turn your back on a fire that is too hot, and looked up at Lyra with her bright eyes.
"Where is he?"
Lyra took her to the side vault.
Corin was sitting up. He had been sitting up since the seventh bell, on his stone bench under the skulls of the old monks, with his back against the wall and the stiff leg out along the bench in its splints and its fresh linen, and the Ledger open on his good knee. He had washed. Silas had brought him a basin and a rag and a sliver of yellow soap at dawn, and he had scrubbed the last of Vespera's paint off his face and his hands until the skin was raw, and now he was himself again. Thin, and gray, and very tired, with the dark straight eyebrows and the mole under the left eye, and the Ash on his hands going gray all the way from the fingertips to above the wrists, where it disappeared up his sleeves.
He looked up as they came in under the arch.
And Lyra saw his face do the thing it did when somebody he knew came into a room. The thing she had watched it learn to do, over the weeks. First nothing. A stranger's look. Polite, and careful, and a little afraid. And then his eyes went down, quickly, to the Ledger, to the page he kept open on his knee for this, the page of faces. And then up again. And then—
Then his mouth went down at the left corner.
"Juno," he said.
Juno stood in the arch of the vault and looked at him. At the stiff leg along the bench. At the splints. At the gray hands on the Ledger.
"You look terrible," she said.
"I know."
"Worse than on the barge. And you looked terrible on the barge."
"I know."
Juno came into the vault, on the sides of her feet, and stood by the bench and looked down at him for a long moment, with her fists at her sides.
Then she sat down on the floor beside the bench, the way Gideon sat, with her back to the wall. And took off her cap. And put it in her lap. And said, in a voice that was nearly steady:
"I've brought you two papers. One from Gran. And one from nobody."
Two Papers
She told it the way she told everything. Fast, and all in a heap, with the important parts tumbling out between the unimportant ones like apples out of a split sack, so that you had to pick them up one by one as they rolled past.
Hessa had put her ashore at Withy Reach last night, at the end of the peat cuttings, by a stone where the cattle came down to drink. Hessa had not wanted to. Hessa had said that a girl who could not walk had no business going anywhere, and Juno had said she could walk, and stood up off the bunk to show her, and fallen over. And then stood up again. And Hessa had looked at her for a long time with her arms folded, and then said Slower, the way she said it to everything, and lifted her over the side herself.
"And Wat carried me to the stone," said Juno. "Through the reeds. In the dark. With his bad shoulder. And Hessa held the lantern. And Robin was asleep in the basket by the tiller with his fist in his mouth." She paused. "And your father was asleep too, in the hay. Tapping. I could hear it through the boards, when they lifted the hatch to get me the blanket. Four, two, nine, three. Like rain."
Lyra sat on the floor beside her, with her back to the wall, and listened.
Ellis had come along the cart road an hour later with the straw wain, six horses, piled so high it swayed. He had been to the cuttings already, at dusk, and given Hessa Oren's message by mouth, and she had read it in his face before he said it, and begun to pole the barge north again before he had finished. He had stopped by the stone without being told. He had looked at Juno sitting on it in Hessa's blanket, and then down at her feet, and then he had got down off the wain and picked her up, all without a word, and pushed her into a hole in the straw at the back that he had made for her, a little cave, with a sack over the mouth of it. And then he had driven to the city. All night, at the slow plod of a straw wain, with stops at every lock and every toll gate.
"They poked the straw," said Juno. "At the Brindle toll. With a pole. Not a hook. A pole. It went past my ear." She touched her ear, as if to make sure it was still there. "Ellis was talking to them all the time, about the price of straw and his mare's bad leg and his wife's mother. He didn't stop talking once. They got so bored they let him through just to make him go away."
She had come into the city before dawn today, at the north gate. Ellis had put her down in Gallows Lane, behind the Bridewell, before he went into the stables, where the constables with the iron rods were. And she had gone home.
Not by the street. By the cellars. Under Abner Cole's coal at number sixteen, and through the gap in the wall into the cellar of number fourteen, and up the cellar steps into the back of her grandmother's kitchen, the way Mrs. Marta had come home a week ago.
"And Gran was at the table," said Juno. "Sitting. With the lamp lit. At five o'clock in the morning. Not doing anything. Just sitting, with her hands in her lap, and a piece of paper on the table in front of her." She looked at Corin. "Gran never just sits."
She put her hand inside her coat.
She took out two things, and laid them on the stone bench beside Corin's stiff leg, on the blanket.
The first was a letter. Lyra knew it at once. A page torn from Hessa's ledger, with the faint blue lines and the red margin, folded in three, the way you fold a letter. Not small. Not clever. It was creased and soft from a week in a girl's coat, and stained at one corner with something brown, and on the outside, in Lyra's own hand, fierce and slanting hard to the right, one word.
Ro.
Lyra looked at it.
She did not understand. For a moment she did not understand at all. She looked at her own letter, lying on the blanket, and felt something go cold in her chest.
"You didn't give it to him," she said.
"I did."
"Then why—"
"Wait." Juno held up her hand. "I'm telling it in order. You have to let me tell it in order or I'll forget a bit." She touched the letter with one finger. "This is yours. I gave it to him. And he gave it back."
Lyra did not move.
"At the pump," said Juno. "On Gallows Lane. At the seventh bell. The cadets come down from the Academy every morning in a line, two by two, with a sergeant at the front with a stick, and they go past the pump on their way to the Ministry. Gran told me. Gran knows everything about the street. So I went and waited by the pump with a bucket, like I was getting water, and when they came by I looked for him. Tall. Dark. Like you, Gran said, but a boy." She sniffed. "He was at the back. On his own. Not two by two. Everybody else had somebody, and he didn't."
"And?"
"And I stepped out in front of him, and held it out, and said, Cadet Thorne. From your sister."
The crypt was very quiet. Out in the main hall, Mrs. Doyle was saying something kind and loud to somebody who did not answer.
"He stopped," said Juno. "In the middle of the street. The whole line went on without him, and the sergeant shouted. And he just stood there and looked at it. In my hand. For ages." She swallowed. "And then he took it. And he didn't open it. He turned it over and looked at the front, at the Ro. And he went white. Whiter than the snow."
"And then he gave it back to you."
"No. Then he put his hand inside his coat." Juno touched her own chest, flat, over the heart. "Here. And took out another one. An old one. All crumpled. Cream paper, the cheap kind. With a brown mark on it." She looked at Lyra. "Like blood. Old blood. And your writing on the front of that one too. Ro. The same."
Lyra did not say anything. She could not.
She knew that letter. She had written it a year ago, just after Midwinter, in the little cold room under the roof where she had lived since the house was sold, by the light of a candle end. She had written one every month, for a year and more, and sent them all to the Academy, and none of them had ever been answered, and she had stopped. And she had thought, she had always thought, that he burned them.
"He held them both," said Juno. "The old one and the new one. One in each hand. Like he was weighing them. And the sergeant was coming back down the street toward him with his stick, shouting. And Rowan looked at me, and said—"
She stopped. She frowned, getting it exactly right.
"He said, Tell her I'll keep the old one. I can't carry two. And he put the old one back inside his coat. Against his chest. And gave me back the new one. Not opened." Juno touched the letter on the blanket. "This one. And then he said, Noon. Here. I'll have an answer. And then the sergeant got to him and hit him on the back of the legs with the stick, and he went."
The brazier ticked in the arch.
Lyra looked down at the letter on the blanket. Her own letter, that she had written on the barge, nearly a week ago, by the light of Hessa's lamp. Ro. It's me. I'm alive. Father's alive. Folded in three. Not opened.
I'll keep the old one. I can't carry two.
She did not pick it up.
"So I'm to go back at noon," said Juno. "To the pump." She looked at Lyra. "If you want."
"I want."
It came out as a whisper. Juno nodded.
Corin had not said anything. He was looking at the other thing on the blanket.
It was very small. So small that Lyra had not seen it at first, lying beside her letter on the gray wool. A square of waxed paper, folded tight and hard and neat, sharp at every corner. No bigger than a fingernail.
"That's the one from nobody," said Juno. "Gran swept it out from under the bottom stair. Last night. In the dark. She said it was put there by an Inquisitor. A woman. In white." Juno's voice went quieter. "Gran said the woman came to give her back her pie cloth. The one from the wreck. With Kross's compliments. And then she told Gran her stair wanted sweeping."
Corin looked at the little folded square for a long time.
Then he put out his gray hand and picked it up, very carefully, between finger and thumb, and held it up to the lamp.
"Wren," he said.
The Glass
It took Corin a long time to open it.
His fingers were not good any more. Lyra had watched them get worse all week. The Ash had gone past his wrists now, and the gray had a dullness in it that it had not had in the autumn, like the gray of old pewter, and his fingertips were slow and stiff, as if he were wearing gloves that did not fit. He held the little square of waxed paper up close to his face, in the lamplight, and picked at the corner of it with his thumbnail, and it would not come. He tried again. And again.
Nobody offered to help him. Lyra did not. Juno did not. They sat on the floor by the bench and watched him, and did not say anything, because they both knew that if anybody offered he would hand it over at once, and say thank you, and then afterward he would write something in the Ledger about it, small, at the bottom of a page, where he thought nobody would read it.
On the fifth try, the corner lifted.
He unfolded it the way Lyra had seen Elara's clerks unfold a document in the autumn, at the Bank, in the Ledger. One fold at a time. Slowly. Counting under his breath. She heard him. Three. Four. Five. He did not need to count. He was counting because he could. Because he still could, up to nine, and past nine it went soft and gray and slipped away from him like a fish. Nine. He stopped. His lips moved and nothing came out. Then he went on unfolding without counting, and the last two folds came open, and the wrapper lay flat on his gray palm.
It was covered in writing.
Lyra could see that from where she sat. Not the words. The words were too small. But the whole of the smooth inside of the wrapper, every corner of it, was gray with marks. Tiny marks. Rows of them. So close and so small that they looked like the grain of the paper, or the pattern on a moth's wing.
Corin held it up to the lamp. He brought it close to his face. He held it away again.
"I can't," he said. "It's too small."
"Silas has a glass," said Lyra. She was already getting up. "For splinters. I've seen it."
The doctor was asleep. He was asleep in the same place as last night, on the floor by the far brazier, with his back against a pillar and his chin on his chest and one boot on and one boot off. Lyra did not wake him. She knelt down beside him and felt in the pocket of his long coat, the left one, where she had seen him put it, and found it. A round glass, the size of the bottom of a cup, in a brass ring, with a short brass handle. Silas murmured something in his sleep. Steady, it sounded like. Steady now. Then he was quiet again.
She took the glass back to the vault.
Corin held the wrapper flat on the Ledger, on his good knee, with one gray finger at each corner. Lyra held the glass over it. She moved it up, and down, until the little gray marks swam up out of the paper and went sharp, and turned into letters.
Small square upright letters. Perfectly even. The kind of hand that a writing master raps your knuckles into, with a ruler, until every loop is the right size.
"Read it," said Corin. "Please. My eyes—"
Lyra read it.
She read it out loud, slowly, a line at a time, moving the glass along the rows the way you move your finger along a line in a book. Her voice in the stone vault sounded strange to her. Very clear. Very flat. Like a clerk reading out a list in a counting house.
"Midwinter. Ours at the Bourse. Front six. Street four, mounted, Vance. Cinder Lane two. Kitchen yard two. Wet door four, in a boat. Vell."
She stopped.
Corin's face had not moved. But his finger on the corner of the wrapper had pressed down, so hard that the nail went white.
"Go on," he said.
"Roof two. Doors one to twelve, one man each, in her livery." Lyra moved the glass. "Not door three. No post. The Treasurer's. D. S. Own men."
Nobody said anything.
Lyra went on, because she could not stop now. "K. and I in the gallery. White masks. K. at the box at midnight. Clause eleven." She took a breath. "K. knows about a quarter to midnight. I don't know how."
She lowered the glass.
She did not look at Corin. She looked at the wall of the vault, at the iron grille in the niche, and the round brown skulls of the old monks stacked behind it like loaves. She looked at them for a long time.
"Read the rest," said Corin quietly.
She lifted the glass.
"Wick sent to the Health today. I couldn't stop it. I'm sorry."
The vault was very quiet.
"Moll here tomorrow, tenth bell. K. wants me to take the notes." Lyra moved the glass to the very bottom corner of the wrapper, where there was one more mark. One letter. Bigger than the others, very slightly, as if the hand that made it had pressed a little harder, at the end. "W."
She put the glass down on the blanket.
Nobody said anything for a long time.
Then Corin let go of the corners of the wrapper. It did not spring back. It lay flat on the Ledger, on his knee, with all its tiny rows of letters, like a moth that has been pinned.
"Door three," he said.
Lyra had already reached under the bench. Her fingers found the box, by Corin's boots, where she had pushed it last night. She pulled it out, and untied the gray silk ribbon, and lifted the lid, and the tissue, layer by layer. And took out the mask, and turned it over, and held it in the lamplight with the lining up, so that he could see.
The tiny gray diamonds. The gold thread. And in the middle, over the bridge of the nose, where the key had been, the ring of double stitches, and the twelve knots of gold, and the two lines.
She tilted it to the lamp until it caught.
"A quarter to midnight," she said.
Corin looked at it. Then, without a word, he opened the Ledger to the page where the little brass key lay pressed flat between the leaves, with its worn bow and its bright new teeth and its V and its 3, and turned the book on his knee so that Juno could see it too. And Lyra told her, in four sentences, about the box, and the footman, and the gold thread, and the man with the watch he never looked at.
Juno, on the floor beside the bench, looked at it too. She had not said a word since Wren. She leaned forward now, with her cap in her lap, and looked at the white mask in Lyra's hands, and the little gold clock in its lining, and her mouth came slowly open.
"That's not fair," she said.
Lyra looked at her.
"It's not fair," said Juno again. "Is it. It's two of them. Playing the same game. With you in the middle." She looked from the mask to the wrapper and back. "The Treasurer sends you a key to door three, and a clock that says when. And Kross takes all the guards off door three, because the Treasurer asks him to. And Kross knows when." She stopped. "So either they're working together. Or one of them knows what the other one's doing, and the other one doesn't know he knows."
Corin looked at her for a long moment.
Then his mouth went down at the left corner.
"Juno," he said, "you should be on the Archon's Council."
"I can't read past my letters."
"Neither can half of them."
Juno did not smile. She sat with her cap in her lap and looked at the mask.
Lyra put it back in the box, face down, with the clock on top. She laid the tissue over it. She did not tie the ribbon.
"Which?" she said. "Which is it?"
"I don't know." Corin picked up the wrapper from the Ledger, very carefully, by its edges, and laid it between two pages, beside the brass key with the V and the 3 on it, and closed the book over all of them. "I don't know. And that's the worst of it. Because if they're working together, the door's a trap. And if they're not—" He stopped.
"If they're not?"
"If they're not, it's still a trap." He put his gray hand flat on the Ledger. "Just not for us."
